To importune someone means to ask them for something repeatedly, urgently, and persistently — in a way that becomes annoying, uncomfortable, or burdensome for the person being asked.

It's not just asking once. It's asking, being turned down or ignored, and asking again — and again — often with increasing pressure, until the other person feels harassed or worn down.

Think of it as having three key ingredients all happening at the same time:

1. Repetition — The asking doesn't stop after one try. The person keeps coming back with the same request.

2. Urgency or pressure — There's a pushy, desperate, or forceful quality to it. The person isn't asking politely and leaving it at that. They're leaning in.

3. It bothers the other person — The one being asked feels pestered, burdened, or even trapped. Their "no" or their silence isn't respected.

If any one of these is missing, you might just have someone who is persistent or eager. All three together? That's importuning.

• "He importuned his landlord for weeks to fix the leaking roof."
    → He asked again and again in a pressuring way, even after the landlord kept putting it off.
  • "She was constantly importuned by her nephew for loans he never repaid."
    → The nephew kept coming back, asking for money in a way she found exhausting and hard to refuse.
  • "The young artist importuned every gallery owner in the city until one finally agreed to display his work."
    → He pressed each one persistently and urgently, not taking no for an answer.
  • "Beggars importuned the tourists at every corner of the marketplace."
    → They approached people repeatedly and urgently, pleading for money in a way that felt overwhelming.
What Makes It Different From Similar Words

These words are all in the same neighborhood, but they're not identical:

  • Ask — Neutral. One time. Polite. No pressure implied.
  • Beg — Emphasizes pleading and desperation, but doesn't necessarily mean it's repeated or annoying.
  • Nag — Repeated criticism or reminding, usually about duties or obligations ("Stop nagging me to clean my room"). It's often used between people in close relationships.
  • Pester — Repeated, trivial, irritating bothering — like a child poking you on a long car ride. It's lighter and often not about anything serious.
  • Badger — Aggressive and relentless pressure to make someone do something — closer to importune, but feels more confrontational and forceful.
  • Harass — Broader, more hostile, and often used in serious or legal contexts.
  • Importune — Sits above most of these in formality, and specifically carries the sense of urgent, persistent requesting that puts the other person in an uncomfortable position. It often implies the asker is willing to sacrifice dignity or social grace in order to get what they want.

When you importune someone, there's a specific social imbalance happening. The person being importuned often feels:

  • Trapped, because refusing feels uncomfortable
  • Pressured, because the other person won't let it go
  • Fatigued, because the repeated asking wears them down

The person doing the importuning is, in a sense, choosing their want over the other person's comfort. That's why the word carries a slightly negative and judgmental flavour — it implicitly criticizes the person doing the asking.
Register: When and Where This Word Is Used

This is an important practical note. Importune is a formal, literary word. You will encounter it in:

  • Classic and contemporary literature
  • Formal essays or journalism
  • Historical or legal texts
  • Elevated or careful writing

In everyday casual speech, people rarely say "importune." Instead they'd say "he kept pestering me" or "she wouldn't stop bugging me about it."

However, knowing this word allows you to use it precisely in your writing, and to recognize it without confusion whenever you encounter it in reading.
The Grammar: How To Use It

The most common pattern is:

importune + [person] + for + [thing]
→ "She importuned her manager for a promotion."

Or simply:

importune + [person]
→ "He would not stop importuning her." (The thing being requested is understood from context.)

You can also use it in the passive voice:
→ "He was constantly importuned by salesmen."

• Importunate (adjective) — Describes a person or behaviour that is characterized by importuning. "His importunate requests exhausted everyone around him." An importunate person is someone who habitually pesters others with urgent, relentless demands.
  • Importunity (noun) — The act or quality of importuning; persistent, tiresome pressure. "Despite her importunity, he refused to change his decision."
  • Importunately (adverb) — "She asked importunately, again and again, for just one more chance."

To importune = to pester someone with repeated, urgent, uncomfortable requests — pushing past hints, refusals, or silence until the word itself makes the asker sound pushy, undignified, and burdensome.
